title: The Unsaid Postcards
premise: Oscar Kavanagh, a translator who has spent thirty years erasing herself between languages, returns to the coastal town of Puerto Sombra when her late mother's house is auctioned by a cousin she barely knows. Sorting through boxes, she finds unsent postcards in her mother's hand addressed to a man named Tomás Reyes—the town's disgraced former judge—revealing that her mother spent years quietly paying off debts for neighbors wronged by Tomás's corrupt rulings. As Oscar traces the postcards' recipients, she uncovers her mother's vigilante ledger of restitution and must decide whether to expose Tomás, now a beloved civic patriarch, or continue her mother's unfinished work. In the end, Oscar chooses neither silence nor scandal: she reads the postcards aloud at the auction itself, letting the town judge its own history, and forgives both her mother and herself before the last word of her childhood language slips away.
about_author: Ada Villalobos is a former court interpreter from the Gulf Coast who writes about the spaces where law fails and memory intervenes. The Unsaid Postcards is her third novel and the first written after her mother's death.

chapters.title: The Smile That Ends Conversations
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. In her city apartment, Oscar translates a corporate report while deliberately forgetting words of her childhood tongue, treating each loss as hygiene. A letter arrives: the house on Calle Luna will be auctioned in six weeks. Emotional beat: controlled detachment cracking at the edges.

chapters.title: Return Ticket, One Way
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. She takes the bus to Puerto Sombra, rehearsing small talk and deploying her perfected smile against curious neighbors. The house is boarded, salt-eaten, exactly as she left it. Emotional beat: dread disguised as efficiency; grief waiting behind every locked door.

chapters.title: Inventory of a Stranger
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Cataloguing belongings for the estate sale, she finds a shoebox of unsent postcards, all addressed to Tomás Reyes, all stamped, none mailed. The handwriting is unmistakably her mother's. Emotional beat: vertigo—the discovery that her mother had an entire life she never narrated.

chapters.title: The Man Everyone Loves
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. At the town plaza she watches Tomás Reyes, retired judge, celebrated philanthropist, accept a plaque. He greets her warmly, calls her 'Marisol's girl.' His kindness feels like a performance she can't audit. Emotional beat: suspicion blooming inside politeness.

chapters.title: Postcard One: The Fisherman's Net
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV, with the postcard text quoted. The first card describes money left anonymously for Don Efraín, whose boat was seized after a rigged ruling. Oscar visits Efraín's widow, who credits 'an angel.' Emotional beat: first proof that her mother ran a quiet campaign of justice outside the law.

chapters.title: Cousin Rafael's Arithmetic
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. The cousin selling the house explains his debts and his need for the auction proceeds, revealing he knew about the postcards and chose silence to protect his inheritance. Emotional beat: banal complicity; corruption as bookkeeping rather than villainy.

chapters.title: The Ledger in the Wall
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Behind a loose kitchen tile she finds her mother's ledger: names, amounts, dates spanning fifteen years, each entry paired with a case number from Tomás's courtroom. Emotional beat: awe curdling into anger—her mother documented everything except why.

chapters.title: Photographs of a Woman I Didn't Know
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Old photographs show her mother laughing with Tomás at a courthouse picnic, years before the ledger began. Oscar interrogates her own memories and finds them edited. Emotional beat: the past refusing to hold still; the stranger in the photos becoming unavoidable.

chapters.title: Postcard Nine: The Schoolteacher
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. A postcard describes paying a schoolteacher's medical bills after Tomás dismissed her wrongful-termination suit. Oscar tracks down the teacher, now elderly, who remembers 'the woman with the envelope' but never asked questions. Emotional beat: gratitude without understanding; the cost of not asking.

chapters.title: What the Auctioneer Knows
chapters.summary: Auctioneer Delia Cruz's POV. Delia has appraised the house and noticed the tile behind which the ledger hid; she also holds old rumors about Tomás's rulings. She warns Oscar, obliquely, that some buyers are coming for more than property. Emotional beat: the town as a nervous organism with long memory.

chapters.title: Tomás Invites Her to Dinner
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Over lamb and wine, Tomás tells fond stories of Marisol, then says, carefully, 'Your mother believed in settling accounts.' He knows about the ledger—or fears he does. Emotional beat: a duel fought entirely in subtext; power flexing through hospitality.

chapters.title: The Word for Forgiveness
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Trying to translate her mother's postcards into English, Oscar discovers the childhood language has no clean word for forgiveness—only phrases meaning 'to un-tie.' She realizes forgiveness may be a knot-work, not a feeling. Emotional beat: linguistic grief becoming moral insight.

chapters.title: Rafael's Confession
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. Drunk, Rafael admits their mother helped Marisol carry envelopes for years, and that he burned one batch of postcards during a bankruptcy scare. Emotional beat: shame surfacing; family loyalty revealed as shared cowardice.

chapters.title: The Case of the Drowned Boy
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. The ledger's darkest entry: a 1998 ruling blamed a dockworker's son for a drowning that witnesses said involved the harbormaster—Tomás's brother-in-law. Marisol's payments to the boy's mother were the largest in the book. Emotional beat: the stakes turn mortal; exposure becomes dangerous.

chapters.title: Someone Searches the House
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Returning at night, Oscar finds the kitchen ransacked, the tile pried open, the ledger gone. Only the postcards remain, hidden in her car. Emotional beat: fear made physical; the story stops being private.

chapters.title: Delia's Offer
chapters.summary: Delia's POV. Delia reveals she photographed the ledger years ago while appraising, and offers Oscar a choice: sell the images to a journalist, or let the auction bury everything. Emotional beat: temptation framed as pragmatism; justice offered as merchandise.

chapters.title: Confrontation at the Breakwater
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Oscar confronts Tomás at dawn. He confesses partially: his rulings were bought, but claims Marisol's restitution was their pact—his guilt laundered through her mercy. He begs her to let the dead stay buried. Emotional beat: the climax of moral ambiguity; no clean villain, only damage.

chapters.title: Reading the Unsent
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. The morning of the auction, instead of letting the house pass silently, Oscar stands on the porch and reads the postcards aloud to the assembled town—names, amounts, apologies intact. Silence, then the drowned boy's mother steps forward. Emotional beat: catharsis; private grief detonated into communal reckoning.

chapters.title: The Verdict of the Town
chapters.summary: Multiple brief POVs—Efraín's widow, the teacher, Delia. The town does not riot or forgive neatly; some spit at Tomás's gate, others defend him, the plaque comes down anyway. Emotional beat: justice rendered imperfectly, by ordinary people, outside any courtroom.

chapters.title: What the House Sold For
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. The house sells for less than expected; Oscar gives her share to the families in the ledger, keeping only the postcards and photographs. Rafael, sobered, asks to help distribute the rest. Emotional beat: restitution completed; money transformed back into meaning.

chapters.title: Un-Tying
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. At her mother's grave, Oscar speaks aloud in the fading childhood language, deliberately using the last words she still owns, then lets them go. She forgives the woman in the photographs—not for the secrecy, but for the courage inside it. Emotional beat: mourning resolved into tenderness.

chapters.title: The First Postcard Sent
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV, epilogue. Back in the city, Oscar writes a new postcard—to Tomás, in prison awaiting trial, saying only 'The account is open. Settle what you can.' She mails it unstamped, the way her mother never dared. Emotional beat: quiet hope; the cycle of unsaid things finally broken.
